# Airline Pricing and Competition in Brazil

<p style="font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace; font-size:.8rem; letter-spacing:.02em;">
Industrial organization · Natural experiments · Instrumental variables · Logit demand · Bertrand-Nash · Merger simulation · Python · 7 tests
</p>
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## The business question

Three airlines carry almost every domestic passenger in Brazil. When a carrier leaves a route,
how much do the fares of those who stay go up? When a new one arrives, do the incumbents cut
prices? And if two of the three merged, which routes would pay for it, and how much? In January
2025 Azul and Abra, the controller of Gol, signed a memorandum to study a combination that
would have held about 60% of the domestic market; the talks ended in September 2025, with
Abra saying the idea still had merit. The question is alive for regulators, airports, travel
buyers and the carriers themselves.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## The data

ANAC, the civil aviation agency, publishes every domestic fare sold to the public each month
and how many seats were sold at it. This case reads **89 months, January 2019 to May 2026:
42.7 million fare lines and 217.9 million seats**. The files changed header, encoding and
decimal mark several times; the loader reads them all and a quality table records each one.
ANAC's traffic statistics add paid passengers, seats offered, fuel burned, distance and
departures for every route, carrier and month. Fares are deflated by the IPCA to 2025 reais.

Two limits come with the source. The fare files cover public sales only, about 27% of paid
passengers; corporate deals, miles and free tickets are not in them, so the fare is the price
of a public ticket, not the average revenue per passenger. And a market here is an airport
pair, so Congonhas and Guarulhos are different markets.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Try it

Pick one of the 60 busiest routes. See each carrier's fare, passengers and the cost and margin
the model implies; start a price war and watch the rivals answer; merge two carriers; or let
a low-cost entrant in. The price sensitivity can be set to the central estimate or to either
end of the range the specifications give.

::: {.rh-section}
## Method

**Natural experiments first.** Avianca Brasil collapsed in the first half of 2019; ITA flew
from mid-2021 until it stopped in December 2021. Each event is measured by difference in
differences on the fares of the carriers that stayed: routes where the event carrier had a
meaningful share against routes it never served, with carrier-route and month fixed effects,
passenger weights and errors clustered by route.

**Demand with instruments.** Passengers choose a carrier on the route or not to fly it, in a
logit model (Berry, 1994) estimated on 164 routes and 392 carrier-route products from January
2022 to May 2026. Fixed effects for each carrier on each route absorb lasting quality, and month
effects absorb seasons. Price is endogenous: fares rise when demand is strong, which is why
ordinary least squares finds almost no response to price. The instruments shift price without
moving this route's demand: the same carrier's fare per kilometre on its other routes that month
(a Hausman-type cost instrument), the number of carriers on the route and the rivals'
frequency.

**Competition as a game.** Each carrier sets its fare to maximize profit given the others', a
Bertrand-Nash equilibrium with differentiated products. Its first-order condition gives the
margin each carrier must have and, from the observed fare, the marginal cost it implies.
A merger changes who owns what, an exit removes a carrier, an entry adds one; new equilibria
are found by iterating the first-order conditions.

**A test before the forecast.** Before simulating a merger, the model is asked to predict the
fares that followed Avianca Brasil's exit, using only the first quarter of 2019.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Results

**When Avianca Brasil left, rivals' fares spiked, then settled a little higher.** On the 50
routes where it had at least 10% of passengers, the fares of those who stayed rose 15% in April,
22% in May and 19% in June 2019 against control routes, while flights were cancelled and seats
disappeared. From July to December the difference was 3.0% (95% interval -3.0% to 9.3%), not
distinguishable from zero.

**ITA's year is too short to say much.** On the 9 routes where it had at least 5% of passengers,
rivals' fares moved 6.8% while it flew (interval -17% to 38%) and 21.9% in the months after it
stopped (interval -6% to 58%). The direction fits the story; nine routes cannot confirm it.

**Price matters once it is instrumented.** Least squares gives a price coefficient of 0.034 per
hundred reais, which would make every carrier's demand inelastic. With the instruments the
coefficient is 0.276 (standard error 0.048, first-stage F of 154), and the median carrier faces
an own-price elasticity of -1.35. The estimate depends on the instruments: adding a fuel-cost
shifter gives 0.285, treating frequency as given gives 0.171, the Hausman instrument alone gives
0.036, and the overidentification test rejects in every case with several instruments. A
nested logit that would let carriers be closer substitutes for each other than for not flying
gave a nesting parameter below zero, outside the model, so the plain logit is used. The
simulator lets the visitor move between 0.171 and 0.285.

**The model passes the Avianca test.** Removing Avianca Brasil from the first-quarter 2019
equilibrium, the model predicts a 3.3% rise in the fares of those who stay, against the 3.0%
observed in the second half of the year. With the lowest price sensitivity it predicts 5.2%.
The observed interval is wide, so this is a consistency check, not a proof.

**A merger of two large carriers.** On the routes where both carriers fly, over the twelve
months to May 2026, with the central estimate:

| Merger | Routes | Fares of the merging carriers | Fares of the rivals | Passengers | Consumer surplus per month |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Azul + Gol | 51 | +12.9% | +0.7% | -5.1% | -R$ 127 million |
| Azul + LATAM | 43 | +12.1% | +0.8% | -5.3% | -R$ 126 million |
| Gol + LATAM | 105 | +19.5% | +1.0% | -12.7% | -R$ 525 million |

Across the range of price sensitivity, the Azul and Gol fares rise between 12.5% and 20.5%. The
passenger change does not depend on that choice, a property of the logit with costs recovered
from margins; the fare change in reais and the loss of surplus do. Rivals barely move because
the logit makes them compete with everyone equally; a model with closer substitutes would
raise their response.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Limits

The fare is the public-sale fare, a minority of passengers. The model sees monthly averages,
so it ignores how fares change as departure approaches and how carriers manage seats. The
instruments disagree with each other, which the overidentification test shows; the range of
results is reported rather than hidden. Costs come from the pricing model, not from accounts:
they are positive for 77% of carrier-routes, and margins look large (a median of 75% of the
fare), which says the marginal cost of one more passenger on a scheduled flight is small,
not that the airlines are profitable. Mergers also change networks, frequencies and costs,
which this model holds fixed.
:::

## Applied to your business

This is the
<a href="../oquant.html#packages">Custom Forecasting package</a> applied to competition and
price. For an airline, an airport, a travel buyer, a bus or logistics operator, or a
regulator, the same tools measure how your fares respond to rivals, what an entry or an exit
does to a route, and what a merger would do before anyone signs it.
:::

## Code

```{=html}
<p>
<a class="rh-btn" href="https://github.com/rhozon/brazil-airline-competition">github.com/rhozon/brazil-airline-competition</a>
</p>
```

With Python 3.11 or later and ANAC's files in `BAC_RAW` (the fare files come from ANAC's
DataSAS download page, one zip per year; the traffic file from ANAC's open-data portal):

```bash
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest -v
python -m bac.cli load       # fare files and traffic statistics
python -m bac.cli analyse    # events, demand, equilibrium, mergers
```

References: ANAC, microdata of domestic fares sold and air transport statistics; Berry
(1994), *Estimating Discrete-Choice Models of Product Differentiation*, RAND Journal of
Economics; Nevo (2001), *Measuring Market Power in the Ready-to-Eat Cereal Industry*,
Econometrica; Peters (2006), *Evaluating the Performance of Merger Simulation: Evidence from the
U.S. Airline Industry*, Journal of Law and Economics.
:::
